sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: Define attitude.
questions.answer: A favourable or unfavourable evaluation of people, objects, ideas and situations.

questions.q: Name the three components of attitude.
questions.answer: Cognitive, affective and behavioural.

questions.q: State true or false: (i) Attitudes are held for a short period of time. (ii) Attitudes provide us with a sense of self.
questions.answer: (i) False. (ii) True.

questions.q: State true or false: (i) Messages that produce anxiety and fear are ineffective. (ii) Strong, personally important attitudes are hard to change.
questions.answer: (i) False. (ii) True.

questions.q: Name the four ways attitudes are learnt.
questions.answer: Direct contact, direct instruction, interaction with others and observational learning.

questions.q: Identify the learning: Amit's father explains why he should stop smoking and Amit stops.
questions.answer: Direct instruction.

questions.q: Define a schema.
questions.answer: A set of interconnected beliefs, information and examples about social objects, events and people.

questions.q: What is confirmatory bias?
questions.answer: The tendency to search for information that supports one's beliefs and to ignore that which does not.

questions.q: What is counterfactual thinking?
questions.answer: Thinking in terms of 'what might have been' about past events.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has four parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: Identify the component: (i) 'He is intelligent and hardworking'; (ii) 'I love cricket'; (iii) 'I will go to meet him'; (iv) which component is the direction and intensity of feeling?
questions.answer: (i) Cognitive. (ii) Affective. (iii) Behavioural. (iv) Affective.

questions.q: Identify the factor of attitude change: (i) the communicator; (ii) the content, clear and fearful; (iii) the receiver; (iv) summarise 'who says what to whom'.
questions.answer: (i) Source. (ii) Message. (iii) Person (target). (iv) Source, message and target person.

questions.q: Name the bias: (i) expecting good events more than others; (ii) attention to negative information; (iii) 'what might have been'; (iv) seeking supporting information only.
questions.answer: (i) Optimistic bias. (ii) Negativity bias. (iii) Counterfactual thinking. (iv) Confirmatory bias.

questions.q: Name any four conditions under which attitudes predict behaviour.
questions.answer: Strong and consistent attitude; awareness of attitude; direct experience; minimal social pressure (also planned, personally relevant behaviour).

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Why do we form attitudes?
questions.answer: They simplify a complicated social world, help understand people and events, define groups and identity and win acceptance.

questions.q: How do attitudes help in identity?
questions.answer: They express a person's values and self-concept, e.g. Gandhi's honesty or Mother Teresa's concern for the poor.

questions.q: How do peers shape attitudes?
questions.answer: We adopt the group's attitudes, and praise and approval from friends reward and strengthen them (instrumental learning).

questions.q: Why is an expert more effective in changing attitudes?
questions.answer: An expert, trustworthy, attractive and similar communicator is believed more, so the receiver changes attitude.

questions.q: Give one reason why attitude may not predict behaviour.
questions.answer: Social or peer pressure, e.g. a boy who dislikes drinking does so because of friends.

questions.q: What are heuristics?
questions.answer: Simple rules used to make complex decisions quickly, such as identifying a 'professor' from typical attributes.

questions.q: Differentiate internal and external attribution.
questions.answer: Internal attribution explains an outcome by personal causes such as effort; external attribution by outside causes such as a tough paper.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain the three components of attitude with an example.
questions.answer: Cognitive (belief that the neighbour is intelligent), affective (liking or disliking his manners) and behavioural (helping him when needed). In strong attitudes the three are consistent.

questions.q: Describe the functions of attitudes.
questions.answer: They help us understand the world and choose whom to approach, describe our social groups, express our identity and values, and win support and acceptance from others.

questions.q: Explain how attitudes are formed.
questions.answer: By direct contact (conditioning), direct instruction by parents and teachers, interaction with others (group and reward), observational learning from models, and through education and media.

questions.q: Explain the factors of attitude change.
questions.answer: Source: expert, trustworthy, attractive, similar. Message: clear, organised, fear-arousing. Person: strong, complex, important attitudes resist change; advertisers use all three.

questions.q: Explain the relationship between attitude and behaviour.
questions.answer: It is complex; attitudes predict behaviour when strong and consistent, accessible, based on direct experience, free of social pressure and when behaviour is planned and personally relevant.

questions.q: Describe the fundamental attribution error and any two biases.
questions.answer: We attribute others' acts to internal causes and our own to external causes. Optimistic bias expects good events for oneself; negativity bias gives more weight to negative information.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Define attitude, describe its components and functions.
questions.answer: Attitude is a favourable or unfavourable evaluation of people, objects and situations. Components: cognitive, affective and behavioural. Functions: understanding the world, defining groups, expressing identity and values, and gaining acceptance and support.

questions.q: Explain how attitudes are formed and changed.
questions.answer: Formed by direct contact, instruction, interaction with others and observation, and by media. Change depends on source (expert, trustworthy), message (clear, fear-arousing) and person (strong attitudes resist). Congruent change is easier than incongruent.

questions.q: Explain the relationship between attitude and behaviour with the conditions for a strong relationship.
questions.answer: Attitude and behaviour often differ (wanting fitness but not exercising). A strong link exists when attitudes are strong, consistent, easily recalled, formed by direct experience, free of social pressure, and when behaviour is planned and personally relevant.

questions.q: Define social cognition. Explain schemas, heuristics, attribution and biases.
questions.answer: Social cognition is interpreting and remembering social information. Schemas organise information (person, event, role); heuristics give quick decisions; attribution seeks internal or external causes; errors include fundamental attribution error, optimistic bias, negativity bias, counterfactual thinking, confirmatory bias and thought suppression.
